utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminaries were announced; therefore, we will continue to hear the final arguments. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning. Yesterday we left off discussing the campaign and its impact on children in Sarajevo. This is where I will pick up today. By 1994, UNICEF reported that at least 40 per cent of the children in the city had been directly shot at by snipers; 39 per cent had seen one or more family members killed; and 73 per cent had their homes attacked or shelled. That is Exhibit P7171, page 9. In addition to the sniping, the SRK attacked civilians in a shelling campaign that took many forms, including massive bombardments that blanketed the city; sporadic, intentional targeting of civilian areas with just a few shells; and the deployment of modified air bombs. The SRK shells spared no virtually no civilian part of the city. The Prosecution has provided representative examples of each of these forms of shelling in paragraphs 922 to 1002 of its final brief. The SRK shells often targeted residential or commercial areas. The shelling stuck hospitals and people attending funerals, SRK mortars hit civilians during everyday day activities, while collecting or queueing for water, shopping in market-places, or lining up for food or other humanitarian aid. Residential houses, mosques, and cultural landmarks were not spared; instead, they were extensively damaged through VRS bombardments. Examples can be found in Exhibits P1888, P6682, and P7683. After years of shelling with mortars, artilleries, and rockets, General Mladic actually increased the destructive capacity of the SRK in 1994 and 1995 through his deployment of modified air bombs that were indiscriminately launched into residential areas of the city. Mladic and Perisic conceived of these contraptions and it was Mladic's personal approval that was necessary to launch them. The Prosecution would further refer the Chamber to paragraphs 749 to 753 of its brief for a more detailed discussion. Even some of the Defence witnesses acknowledged the terrifying impact of the VRS shelling and sniping directed at the population. Kecmanovic at page 23881 confirmed that it was living with that sense that your city was being randomly showered with shells that terrified you. GRM097, at page 40160, agreed that General Mladic wasn't above using terror as a weapon and targeting civilians. Even Defence expert Kovic admitted to the Chamber at page 41986 that the effect of the campaign in Sarajevo was terrorising. Turning to the Defence brief and its take on the campaign. In its brief, specifically at paragraphs 1327, 1741, and 1800 to 1848, the Defence denies that the SRK did any of this and provides a fictional narrative of the accused's involvement in the events in Sarajevo, one where he is actually the heroic saviour who made consistent attempts to ensure the safety of those in Sarajevo, going as far as to say he ensured "the well-being/welfare" of them. These statements could not be further from the truth. In support of this, the Defence points to a few examples of Mladic's kindness during the campaign. Taking these in turn: The Defence claims in paragraphs 1803 and 1804 that General Mladic offered the airport as a "gesture of goodwill" to ensure the passage of humanitarian aid to the civilians and - in the same paragraph - that he ordered not a single bullet was to be fired at the airport. These submissions are impossible to square with the evidence in this case that shows Mladic and Karadzic continually used humanitarian aid as a tool for leverage. Even after surrendering control of the airport to UNPROFOR, Karadzic threatened UN officials in September 1994 and said that: "In the event the arms embargo was lifted, the Serbs would take UN Blue Helmets hostage, shoot down a lot of planes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- in the event the embargo was lifted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The arms embargo at the time. "Shoot down a lot of planes and arrest all foreigners." That is Exhibit P840. Later that same month, while Mladic was present in Lukavica UNPROFOR reported the VRS had received orders to open fire on all aircraft because Mladic wanted "to show his determination to close the airport and restrain freedom of movement." That's P629. And then, there's evidence of the SRK actually firing on planes, like the occasion in March 1995 where Akashi's plane landed in the airport and the VRS fired on it. That is P872, paragraph 99, and Exhibit P880. This portrayal is also impossible to square with Mladic's own SRK commander's response to protests about the deliberate sniping of civilians crossing the airport. In one such response, Galic expressly told Abdel-Razek that if civilians continued to cross the airport, his side would continue shooting at them. This can be found in P293, paragraphs 91 and 104. That is exactly what happened. When desperate conditions caused more civilians to attempt night-time crossings of the airport in early 1993, anywhere between five to 30 civilians a night were shot by Galic's forces over a two- to three-month period. The shooting of civilians crossing the airport is discussed in greater detail in paragraph 689 of the Prosecution's final brief. This evidence also runs counter to Defence claims in paragraph 1836 regarding the freedom of movement of civilians where they say the civilians of Sarajevo were "always permitted" freedom of movement into and out of SRK-held territory and they were "never blockaded" by the SRK. The reality, of course, was different. General Mladic took pride in this fact, as demonstrated in the intercept mentioned earlier where he stated that he had blocked Sarajevo from four corners, that the city was trapped, and that there was no way out. The reality is that the SRK blocked all the roads into and out of Sarajevo. As already mentioned, civilians ran across the airport in droves, in desperate dashes for freedom, and the SRK shot at them with machine-guns as they did. Access to the narrow tunnel eventually built under the airport was limited and crossing through it was difficult, as Defence witness Radojcic himself acknowledged at page 23112. The lack of freedom of movement for the civilians of Sarajevo is also contradicted by numerous VRS orders, including, Mladic's own directives, which repeatedly ordered the SRK to prevent the de-blockade of the city and to tighten the circle. There are other examples, like the one now appearing before you on the slide. This is Exhibit P6523, an SRK tasking order from April 1994, where Galic instructed SRK units to "fortify positions around Sarajevo by erecting wire and concrete barriers, which would in turn strengthen the belief that they really are blocked (in a camp)." This task obviously applied to both military and civilians within the SRK encirclement. As Colonel Dragicevic acknowledged, it was impossible for the SRK to surround ABiH forces in the city without also surrounding civilians and instilling this camp-like feeling with the use of concrete barriers and wire. This is at pages 23776 to 78. The Defence makes a similarly outlandish claim in paragraph 1817 that Mladic "did not support" or give any orders that obstructed the passage of humanitarian convoys. This Chamber has received overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Mladic controlled and deliberately manipulated the supply of humanitarian aid and utilities throughout the campaign. He did this in order to restrict the flow of humanitarian aid within the city. According to Banbury, the VRS exercised total control over UN convoys, and General Mladic was very obstructive when it came to the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Fraser indicated that Mladic regularly restricted convoys and described how Mladic would sometimes use those convoys as pawns, as he "would run you down to your last day of food, water, fuel, then show you who was in control by allowing a convoy in." That's P576, paragraph 137. Another example Fraser provided was when Mladic threatened to restrict convoys into Sarajevo if there was no apology for recent NATO air-strikes. When no apology came, Mladic closed all check-points into Sarajevo. This is at transcript page 5774. The Defence next claims in paragraphs 1827 to 1829 of its brief that General Mladic took "every action" to ensure the supply of water, gas, and electricity to Sarajevo; and that "no orders were ever given" for the supply of services into the ABiH areas of Sarajevo to be severed. These Defence claims are flatly contradicted by the voluminous evidence in this case. Mladic himself even issued such orders. On the slide before you is now one such order. In Exhibit P7406, General Mladic unambiguously orders "immediately stop supplying water, electricity, and gas to the Muslim part of Sarajevo." So orders were, in fact, given and they came from the accused. Also, everyone understood how the VRS was using the utilities in Sarajevo, even local Bosnian Serb officials. For example, in P6714, the Serbian City Assembly of Sarajevo complained to RS officials about the damage caused to local Serbian households from "the most recent using of Sarajevo for the purpose of raising and lowering tensions in the whole of former Bosnia and Herzegovina (the cutting-off of electricity, water, and gas)." Likewise, the Defence's contention in paragraph 1809 that Mladic repeatedly offered to demilitarise Sarajevo and place all heavy weapons under the control of UNPROFOR is not accurate. This contention is invalidated by the circumstances, which include orders that subverted the relocation of weapons and show the offers were not made in good faith. The evidence shows that the Main Staff only agreed to the Total Exclusion Zone, or TEZ, as part of a number of military and humanitarian concessions to avoid threatened NATO attacks following Markale I. The evidence also shows that the SRK had no intent to actually implement the TEZ. As internal orders reveal, they planned to remove inoperative weapons while hiding the operative ones. Orders from the Main Staff and SRK expressly refer to the relocation of weapons in 1994 as a "diversionary tactic" and also state the inoperative weapons were removed "in order to give the Military Observers the impression that they were withdrawing our heavy weapons." Theses are references to P730 and P4428. Another example is P2249. Moreover, the reduction of shelling after Markale 1 was accompanied by a spike in sniping. By 19 March 1994, the level of sniping in the city was increasing. Both Thomas and RM164 testified that after the creation of the TEZ sniping became a more pronounced component of the campaign. The SRK resorted to this increased sniping against the civilian position, because at that time they temporarily lost their advantage of their heavy weapons. Now the Defence also cites VRS orders at various points in its brief and argues that these orders somehow show some type of reduced culpability or exculpatory behaviour by the accused. For example, in paragraph 2437 of its brief, the Defence states that Mladic "strictly prohibited any offensive fire and implemented an absolute ban on the targeting of civilians." They then refer he to a few of Mladic's own orders. We will now look at one of them. This is Exhibit P812 on the screen before you. It is one of the orders the Defence relies upon in its brief to say that Mladic instituted an absolute ban on offensive fire and targeting civilians. Looking at the text of this order, under item 2, it states that offensive actions cannot be undertaken without the approval of the Main Staff. And under item 3, Mladic states that fire is forbidden on civilians "without my approval." As General Smith at page 7462 succinctly stated, when things are based on the approval of the superior command "that is not the same as banned." These are not complete prohibitions or even remotely exculpatory orders. What they do show is that Mladic's approval was necessary for firing on the civilians of Sarajevo, which is how the VRS worked. These kind of orders are addressed in greater detail from paragraphs 637 to 644 and 646 to 650 of the Prosecution's final brief. As can be seen from these sections of our brief, the documents the Defence relies upon either represent Mladic's modulation of the campaign or his attempts to deny or deflect international criticism. Although the Defence tries to paint the picture of the accused as a kind man who cared about civilians, as the Prosecution has shown, the evidence in this case tells an entirely different story. As Mladic himself bragged during the interview mentioned by Mr. Tieger earlier: "Whenever I come by Sarajevo, I kill someone in passing. That's why the traffic for Sarajevo was disrupted ... snipers. I go, kick the hell out of the Turks, who gives a fuck for them!" That's P1974. As Mladic's own words made clear, he didn't care about the well-being of Muslims in Sarajevo. Also, as Harland explained at pages 724 to 725, there was a direct connection between General Mladic's statements and the effects on the ground. So given Mladic's own words and his actions where he directed attacks on the civilian parts of Sarajevo, there is no wonder that life for civilians in the city was, in the words of Banbury, almost unbearable. While describing the accused as a benevolent commander who constantly controlled SRK fire by restricting it and who ensured the freedom and well-being of everyone, the Defence shifts at times to a depiction of the SRK as a reactionary force with little or no means available to it. These arguments taken together are basically asking you to find that Good Samaritan Mladic was doing all he could with what little he had in the SRK. This depiction of the SRK doesn't hold up either. In fact, the Defence's false narrative about the SRK falls flat on its face from the outset. In paragraph 1714, as part of its attempt to say the SRK was at a distinct disadvantage to the ABiH, the defence mistakenly argues that the formation of the SRK came in response to the ABiH's establishment in Sarajevo. They rely on expert Kovac for this proposition; however, Kovac - their military expert - couldn't even get incredibly basic information on the formation of the opposing forces correct and he was confronted at page 41605 with Exhibit P7676, an order showing that the ABiH was actually formed after the SRK, not the other way around. Contrary to the Defence's claims in paragraphs 1711 to 1712 and 1717 to 1725, the SRK was not an under-manned, under-trained, and under-equipped force compared to the ABiH. General Wilson said at pages 4008 to 4011 that the SRK was well-equipped, very well organised, and fought professionally. This was also the SRK's own view of itself, as illustrated in P6543, where in January 1995, General Milosevic commended the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade for being a highly organised and effective force throughout its long history of military successes. By comparison, it was the ABiH 1st Corps in Sarajevo that was ill-equipped and disorganised. General Wilson described the ABiH forces at page 3922 to 26 as a rag-tag bunch at the beginning of the war and far from a competent force. Although the ABiH improved over time, Konings said that, even in 1995, the ABiH was not a professional army. That's P1741, paragraph 28. And contrary to the Defence submissions, the SRK and the RS MUP were well aware during the conflict that the ABiH was inferior. For example, in 1993, 1st Smbr member Desimir Sarenac reported in P6790 that discipline in the ABiH was non-existent. The men were unruly and they had no uniforms. In P6769, the RS MUP reported that same year that the ABiH forces were "in disarray, MTS provisions are very poor, and they have nothing to offer in resistance to the far better armed VRS units." And lastly, in 1995, SRK Colonel Marko Lugonja reported in D1273 that the ABiH was unreliable and weak in combat. Also contrary to the Defence assertions, the SRK possessed superior weaponry over the ABiH, a fact that even Defence witnesses confirmed. In both his statement and at pages 23868 and 23872 Kecmanovic stated that Serb artillery was superior to the ABiH artillery. General Milovanovic, the accused's immediate subordinate, indicated at pages 17101 to 02 that the SRK had the advantage in heavy weapons. And again even Defence expert Kovic stated in his report at page 62 of D1369 that the Serbs maintained their heavy weapon advantage in Sarajevo until the end of the war. Finally, the aforementioned Desimir Sarenac admitted at page 26179 that it was "widely known" that the ABiH had a shortage of ammunition and weapons. The discrepancy between the limited weaponry in the city and the SRK heavy weapons in the surrounding hills was aptly described by volunteer fire-fighter John Jordan, who said: "The violence in and around Sarajevo was basically shovelled downhill and spooned uphill." Transcript page 1824. One of the more blatantly false statements about the SRK comes in paragraph 2098, where the Defence states "at no stage during the conflict" did the SRK have trained snipers or use them. The SRK had snipers, and the evidence shows that the SRK sniping was actually part of an organised and centralised effort to target the civilian population. For example, the VRS prominently discussed its snipers in the 1992 VRS combat-readiness report, Exhibit P338. On page 10, in the section on command and control, the organised training of scouts and snipers is described as one of the most important elements for the combat-readiness of the army. Another is Exhibit P677, which is now coming onto the screen before you. This is the 1995 VRS Main Staff programme for snipers, and it shows just how central the Main Staff was to their instruction. Right at the beginning of the document, the Main Staff states that sniper courses are organised at the corps command level, and they were held several times a year. This regular sniper training provided "high-grade professional training," and snipers received instruction on seven subjects, including the effect of a sniper in a populated area. As these materials demonstrate, not only was there training of snipers, but it was the Main Staff who oversaw and ensured SRK snipers maintained their lethal capabilities. The fact that SRK brigades possessed trained snipers and kept training them throughout the campaign is something you can also see in the documents from the individual SRK brigades. For instance, the 1st Romanija Brigade possessed and trained snipers from the beginning of the war. This can be found in P6543. And this same brigade specifically reported on 29 October 1993 that "over the spring period we trained all snipers from the lower units." That is P676. Defence witness Vlade Lucic, a former member of the 1st Romanija Brigade, even admitted his brigade had snipers "per establishment." This is in D658, paragraph 25. The Defence also makes claims in paragraph 2100 of its final brief that "no orders were ever given" to snipe civilians; and that no orders were ever received by any member of the SRK to this effect. These arguments make no sense in the context of Mladic's own acknowledgment in March 1995 to General Smith that the SRK's increase of sniping of civilians was in response to Serb casualties from an ABiH attack. That is Exhibit P876, page 4, and transcript page 8222. Also during March 1995, in P7809, a UNMO patrol was present when a 1st Romanija Battalion commander ordered his subordinate to fire on anything that moved, whether they were soldiers or civilians. In P7810, the same UNMO patrol confirmed this battalion commander's order when it was echoed by SRK soldiers on the front line, who told the UNMOs that they will open fire on anybody who moves, including women and children. At the end of the day, the Defence has to run away from acknowledging the existence of SRK snipers during the campaign because there is no justification for how the SRK used them. As Banbury stated, "there was no reason for the Serbs to be sniping in Sarajevo. There were no military targets suitable for sniping." He then emphasised the fact that civilians, including women, children, and the elderly, were regularly victims of sniping. Van der Weijden explained the effect of snipers and stated: "A victim killed by a sniper only affects the victim and the people in the direct vicinity, but the thought of never being safe from the enemy affects everybody. Apart from being shot at, the anxiety mainly comes from not knowing where or how or exactly when the sniper will strike." In other words, the only explanation for SRK sniping civilians was that it was intended to inflict terror amongst the population. The Prosecution at this time is going to address one unscheduled shelling that the Defence raises on a number of occasions in its brief. It's the Vase Miskina shelling on 27 May 1992. Like many other instances, the Defence theory on this shelling is not clear, vacillating between unsupported conspiracy theories, involving staged explosions with a planted device and unfounded accusations that the ABiH were the ones who fired the mortar. Contrary to the Defence assertions in paragraphs 1885 to 1905 of its brief, the shelling of the bread line on Vase Miskina Street is not part of Scheduled Incident G1. This was acknowledged by the Defence at transcript page 39134. For this shelling, the Defence relies on former SRK member Bukva in paragraph 1869, whose claims about the Vase Miskina shelling were based on intelligence from some unknown source that the BiH authorities staged the event by planting an explosive device. This planted device theory, which has no support, is then contradicted and not relied upon five pages later in the Defence brief where the Defence states in paragraph 1891 that the explosion "could only have been" caused by an incoming projectile. In this later discussion, the Defence abandons its previous explosive device theory. They instead rely on the content of Zorica Subotic's report and her twisted attempt to place almost all of the firing positions within ABiH territory based upon an almost vertical angle of descent of 83 or 84 degrees. This discussion completely ignores what happened during her testimony in court. With respect to the Vase Miskina shelling, Subotic's opinion was exposed at pages 39597 to 39602 through her admission that her co-author intentionally altered a photo from the investigative file. This was done in order to make the crater appear like an almost perfectly spherical shape, consistent with a high incoming angle. Her claim that there was no on-site investigation at the time, which was repeated in paragraph 1899 of the Defence brief, was wrong. The official investigation report admitted as part of D1243 unmistakably states that an on-site investigation of the crater was done shortly after the shelling. This same investigation report, which Subotic indicated she knew about but nevertheless did not reference as part of her opinion in D2117, undermined her vertical firing theory and showed that the firing points came from a greater distance. Eventually, at page 39609, Subotic conceded that the angle of descent was much lower than the 83 degrees she tried to initially sell to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. In reference to D1243, the same investigation report, which Subotic indicated she knew about but nevertheless did not reference as part of her opinion in D2117, undermined her vertical theory and showed that the firing points came from a greater distance. Eventually at page 39609, Subotic conceded that the angle of descent was much lower than the 83 degrees that she originally presented to this Chamber. The Defence brief relies on Subotic's report as if none of this ever happened. Subotic's vertical firing theory, which would have also required the shot to have been fired in close proximity to the point of impact, is also undermined by the fact that the surviving witnesses who were waiting in the bread queue did not hear an outgoing round before the shell impacted. This can also be found in Exhibit D1243. In paragraph 1897 of its brief, the Defence discusses the intercept related to the Vase Miskina shelling and how it was against Mladic's orders, but they fail to mention the part where Gagovic is informed of the shelling coming from his own SRK forces on Trebevic and where he states in response: "Who the fuck is firing from up there?" They also do not mention Exhibit P4359, Mladic's 27 May order telling all units to be ready to open fire but giving no order to fire during ongoing negotiations related to the barracks evacuations that day. As further detailed in paragraphs 925 to 932 of the Prosecution's brief, Mladic then did order the SRK to carry out a city-wide bombardment of Sarajevo the next day. If anything, this intercept demonstrates how Mladic was central for the approval of all aspects of SRK's mortar use, all the way down to the firing of 82-millimetre mortars. Anyway, with respect to the Vase Miskina shelling, the shell that landed on Vase Miskina Street on 27 May came from the SRK and it was not part of some grand conspiracy or the ABiH launching a shell straight into the air so it could fall on themselves. Lastly, in paragraph 1898 the Defence brief relies on Mladic's denial of the Vase Miskina shelling and his attempt to deflect responsibility through his own self-motivated claims about an investigation. There are no records of investigations into shellings at the end of May and early June 1992; and if there had been investigations at the time, General Mladic would have had to look no further than himself to find someone who was responsible for the bombardments of the city. This brings us to our next topic. Underlying many of the Defence claims are overstated assertions that seek to vilify the ABiH for everything that happened in Sarajevo. These attempts are not new. For example, from paragraphs 1827 to 1835 of its brief, the Defence's attempt to blame utility cut-offs on the Muslims perfectly replicates Mladic's own strategy for hiding his forces' responsibility, as outlined at the 16th Assembly Session. During that speech, he stated that his forces would shut down the electricity, gas, and water in Sarajevo, as he had previously done in Croatia, while wisely telling the world that the Muslims had done it and the Bosnian Serbs were doing the best to repair it. That's P431, pages 38 to 39. As we have seen, the truth was far different and Mladic actually determined whether and how Sarajevo would receive the supply of utilities. The Defence does not stop there. Starting at paragraph 1853 of its brief, the Defence goes as far as to assert that the Bosnian leadership and the ABiH were the true perpetrators of the shelling and sniping campaign conducted against the civilians of Sarajevo, as if the entire three and a half years of SRK shelling and sniping can be justified or explained entirely by the Bosnians firing on their own population. Even the Defence evidence doesn't tell you this. For example, D1425, an Independent newspaper article which the Defence relies upon, in paragraph 1856. This article discusses views expressed by some unnamed UN officials, who emphasised that the suspicions of BiH attacks "were a tiny minority among the regular city bombardments by Serbian forces." As this article also demonstrates, the Defence relies on speculative claims that have routinely been shown throughout this case to be either generic, unsupported, or based on a witness's knowledge of media reports. Ultimately, these speculative claims have proved to be unfounded when exposed to any kind of scrutiny. In many instances, central parts of the Defence narrative are based on non-existent evidence. Take the evidence of VRS propagandist Milovan Milutinovic. In paragraph 1862 of the Defence brief, they rely on Milutinovic's recitation of a direct quote of Martin Bell, who supposedly stated: "I felt like a poor foot soldier in an army whose entire Muslim command lost their mind and terrorised their own people." The problem is Bell never said this. On the slide before you, Milutinovic's quotation of Bell is on the top and the actual quote of Bell is on the bottom. What Bell actually said was: "I felt like a humble foot soldier in an army whose high command had taken leave of their collective senses - and I told them so." On pages 30056 to 58, Milutinovic was confronted with Bell's actual quote, which shows that Bell was actually discussing the actions of his own government, not the Muslim command, and he did not mention any ABiH terrorising of their own people. When asked how on earth he got Bell's quote so wrong, Milutinovic stated he did not speak English and tried to blame the error on a local paper he read in Serbian, ignoring the fact that in his statement he had very misleadingly attributed the direct quote to an English-language newspaper and not to any other source. The Defence also tries to point to specific instances where the ABiH supposedly fired on themselves. The first of these supposed events that the Defence points to can be found in paragraph 1855, where they assert that Captain Hansen told Bosnian officials to stop firing at their own people after the shelling of the RTV building on 28 June 1995. This claim is solely based on the testimony of UNMO Oien. When directly asked about this specific event at page 43196, Oien stated he couldn't tell us about it and: "I don't remember. I was not there and I can't confirm anything of this." In addition to not exactly having an inspiring basis for their assertion, there is ample evidence which the Defence ignores that it was, in fact, the SRK who fired the modified air bomb that impacted the RTV building on 28 June 1995. This is supported by the evidence of witness Brennskag, who saw that modified air bomb launched from the VRS side of the confrontation lines; and also Harland, Banbury, and RM110, and Exhibit P966, P991, P752, P6711, the complete investigative filed admitted as P7572, D203, and D165. Finally the SRK report admitted by the Defence truly underscores the disingenuous nature of these submissions. The SRK in its own report, admitted as Defence Exhibit D147, acknowledged that the SRK were the ones who fired and hit the RTV building on 28 June. They leave mention of this out of their discussion of the shelling. In a related effort with respect to the tram snipings, the Defence tries to rely on D1810. This is that single cherry-picked document from an October 1994 BiH MUP investigative file. The Prosecution tendered the whole file in rebuttal as P7852. This file clearly shows that the information relied upon by the Defence was mistaken and the fire actually came from the SRK positions in Grbavica. In addition to the ballistics evidence in the complete file, the materials reveal that witnesses even heard multiple bursts of fire coming from the SRK positions on this occasion. Then there is Scheduled Incident G4, the shelling of the football match on 1 June 1993 in Dobrinja. On this one, the Defence also claims the ABiH fired the shell. And at paragraph 1946 states: "A number of ABiH artillery positions were located upon the estimated bearing of the projectile, including those within the Toplik area; and it is possible that the projectile could have originated from one of those positions." In support of this, the only witness they cite is John Hamill. The problem is, is that John Hamill was an UNMO on the Lima side, not the Papa side, and the artillery positions in Toplik that he is describing in the referenced part of the testimony belong to the SRK and not to the ABiH. The fact that these were SRK mortar positions in the area of Toplik was also confirmed by SRK Artillery Commander Savo Simic, who even indicated his mortars in the area were pointed towards Dobrinja. The only evidence in the record is that it was the SRK who possessed mortars in the Toplik area. In addition to the false Toplik assertion, the Defence then throws out in the next sentences of the same paragraph the possibility that a mobile mortar was used to launch a shell originating from the same direction. This time they rely on a completely unrelated part of Hamill's testimony that has nothing to do with G4. This whole theory is absurd, but if we could look at a map anyway just to see the supposed route that the ABiH mortar crew would have had to have travelled. This is an annotated cut out of the map marked by John Hamill and admitted as P539. On this map, the road between Dobrinja and Toplik is marked in red. Based on this route, this mobile mortar crew would have had to have driven out of Dobrinja and into SRK territory. They then would have had to have passed through Lukavica, where the SRK command is located, and then continue on to the vicinity of Toplik. This entire area is littered with SRK artillery and mortar positions according to the evidence of Savo Simic. You would think that an ABiH mobile mortar crew pulling up to SRK positions and firing off a couple of shots would have gotten at least a mention in their daily combat report. The combat report from that day has been admitted as D1778. And no, that report states there were no unusual incidents that day. In reality, there is absolute zero evidence that any of this ever took place. For G4, the evidence in this case conclusively shows that the minimum firing distance of the shell places the origin of fire within SRK territory, and this is just a desperate attempt to try to say otherwise. Your Honours, I see that we're at the time for a break and I'm about to head into a new section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Weber. We'll take a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I invite you to proceed. But it would assist us - and I know that the failure is entirely with us, our old ears - that if you would pronounce your words more explicitly, that we would not have to check again and again in the transcript whether we really heard what we thought we may have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That is very kind, Your Honours, but I think the responsibility lies with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Turning to the Scheduled Incidents. The Chamber has received detailed evidence on the snipings and shellings that constitute the scheduled F and G incidents and how these events are representative of what happened throughout the campaign. In its brief, the Defence heavily relies on the reports of its two ballistics experts in its discussion of the Scheduled Incidents. The Prosecution addressed these two witnesses in paragraphs 1049 to 1057 of its brief. At this time, the Prosecution will provide some additional submissions on the unreliability of these witnesses in the context of the Defence brief. Zorica Subotic and Mile Poparic have provided evidence that is not credible in this case. It's particularly telling that the Defence brief has offered numerous citations, hundreds of them, to the written reports of these experts but cited comparatively little to the witness's in-court testimony. The reason is simple: The Defence experts and their opinions did not hold up to scrutiny on the witness-stand. The cross-examination of these experts repeatedly demonstrated that Subotic's and Poparic's theories have no sound basis. When it comes to the Defence's shelling expert, the failings of Subotic stem partly from her lack of experience. As she admitted, she has never analysed a freshly formed crater in person. She has never been to the scene of a mortar explosion immediately after a detonation. In fact, her only experience with crater analysis occurred in 2010, when she prepared her excerpt report for the Karadzic case. This is the same visit that she used as a basis for her opinions in this case. With her limited experience in crater analysis, Subotic decided to then engage in methods that were filled with errors. She analysed craters that had been physically eroded or repaired in the years after the shellings. If the craters had been paved over, she relied on videos and photographs even though that practice could lead to different results, which she admitted at page 39630. Even though Subotic agreed that the best time to conduct a reliable crater analysis was immediately after an impact, she rejected the mortar analyses that ballistics investigators had conducted immediately after the shelling events, disregarding their findings in favour of her own exceptionally belated analysis in 2010, over 15 years after the conflict ended. To reach her discussions, Subotic sometimes even manipulated the evidence in order to absolve the SRK. For example, when she evaluated Scheduled Incident G4, the shelling by the SRK of a football match that was mentioned earlier, Subotic used the grid co-ordinates provided by the UNPROFOR investigation and then plotted those co-ordinates on a different map that she knew used a different grid scale. And the consequences of such a manipulation should be immediately apparent, plotting the same co-ordinates on a different map that uses a different grid scale will lead to a plotting of the event in a new location. Instead of acknowledging that plotting the same co-ordinates on different map with different scales might lead to different results, Subotic claimed that her new plotting discredited UNPROFOR's original investigation. In fact, the result is the opposite. This shows just how much Subotic was willing to manipulate the available evidence to reach the conclusions she sought to achieve. The Defence nevertheless relies on Subotic's manipulation in its brief, asserting the same flawed point in paragraph 1938. Subotic also offered a number of wholly unsupported conspiracy theories to explain the Markale shellings. For example, on Scheduled Incident G8, Markale I, Subotic claimed that a stationary device was set in the market. The Defence brief similarly relies on Subotic's claims in their brief, but Subotic's static explosion theory required a vast conspiracy. Her theory required a professional sabotage team to dig a hole, with the precise measurements needed to make the mortar appear like it came from SRK territory. It required conspirators to plant a stabiliser prior to the static explosion. Her grand theory also required conspirators who brought in bodies to the market after the explosion in order to mimic victims. When asked who was part of this vast conspiracy, Subotic couldn't even name one single person. It was something she just made up. There's also no physical evidence to support her theory of a static explosion; even Subotic acknowledged that. As Gauthier - a Defence witness and head of the UN investigation into the shelling - testified, the Markale I shelling was not caused by a stationary device, but was the result of a 120-millimetre mortar fire. Similarly, GRM065 agreed in D1442 that the incident was not the result of a static explosion. This static explosion theory is also ruled out in the UN investigation file on page 21 of Exhibit P538. Other times, Subotic continued to hold on to specific opinions, even in the face of overwhelming evidence that her opinion was wrong. One example of this was her testimony in relation to Scheduled Incident G10; this is the SRK's modified air bomb attack on Hrasnica on 7 April 1995. Subotic refused to acknowledge the fact that a 250-kilogramme modified air bomb was used in this attack. As a supposed ballistics expert, she refused to acknowledge it even though the ballistics report in the investigative file stated that a fuse from a 250-kilogramme air bomb was found at the scene. She still refused to admit that it was a 250-kilogramme air bomb when informed that the VRS's own documents confirmed that it was a 250-kilogramme air bomb. As if the ballistics information and the contemporaneous documents were not enough, she then continued to deny it was a 250-kilogramme air bomb even after being informed that the Ilidza Brigade Commander Radojcic testified before this Chamber that it was his brigade who indeed fired a 250-kilogramme air bomb at Hrasnica. When it came to Radojcic's testimony, Subotic actually suggested that he wasn't telling the truth, that she knew better than the brigade commander who fired the thing. Subotic held fast to her theory in the face of overwhelming evidence for a very specific reason: She wanted to minimise the destructive capacity of the modified air bomb used from a 250-kilogramme one to that of 100 kilogrammes. Her evidence was an ploy to say that the SRK used a more proportional amount of force against some supposed target. Due to her extraordinary bias and utter lack of credibility, she held on to an entirely unsupported opinion. Her evidence should be rejected. Similar failings and evidence manipulations undermine Poparic, who testified as the Defence's sniping expert on the Scheduled Sniping Incidents. As an initial matter, Poparic admitted that he constructed his line-of-sight arguments without a GPS and he ignored the OTP GPS co-ordinates where victims were sniped because he found the information was not necessary. Consistent with the efforts of Subotic, Poparic also engaged in fabrications and contorted reasoning in his attempts to exculpate the accused. For example, in order to lay blame on the ABiH, Poparic intentionally plotted the location of Scheduled Incident F16 in a different location from where the victim, Tarik Zunic, said he was shot. Instead of relying on Zunic's testimony about the location of the incident, Poparic placed the sniping in another location which was less visible from Spicaste Stijena. The Defence's brief similarly relies on Poparic's manipulation, even though he admitted - that being Poparic - that Zunic's testimony was consistent with other evidence. Poparic instead chose to believe an unnamed couple that he encountered on a visit in 2010, who allegedly told him that the sniping occurred in a different location. There is nothing in evidence supporting Poparic's opinion and the evidence on all points indicate that the shot came from the SRK. Poparic also denied well-known facts. A simple example: In paragraph 2170 of the Defence's brief regarding Scheduled Incident F9, the Defence solely relies on Poparic's unsupported assumption to claim that "the Prosecution failed to prove there was a VRS firing position at the window of the institute for the blind." The Defence's claim is contradicted by its own witness. 1st Battalion commander of the Ilidza Brigade Guzina admitted that the SRK held a position at the school for the blind. This is can be found at transcript page 22548 and D514, paragraph 37. The Defence criticises the ABiH investigators in paragraphs 1876 to 1883 of its brief; however, in contrast to Subotic and Poparic, the BiH investigators - such as Sabljica, Suljevic, Turkusic, Sokolar, Besic, and Miokovic - were experienced investigators who conducted hundreds of investigations during the conflict. More importantly, for all the Defence's claims of bias, the findings of the BiH investigators in the Scheduled Incidents were often corroborated by UNPROFOR investigations. For example, the Scheduled Incident G7, the shelling of humanitarian aid queue in Dobrinja. The BiH investigation determined that the shells came from the east, toward Lukavica; the UNPROFOR investigation likewise corroborated the BiH investigation and found the shells came from the direction of Lukavica. The BiH investigations represent just one part in a mountain of evidence that the Prosecution has presented regarding the terror campaign in Sarajevo. The testimony of witnesses the Chamber heard from throughout this case and the exhibits admitted into evidence lead to only one conclusion: For over three years, General Mladic and the other members of the Sarajevo terror JCE led a campaign of terror against the civilians of Sarajevo. And as a result of that campaign, General Mladic is responsible for the charged crimes of terror, unlawful attacks, and murder. Your Honours, at this time, this concludes my remarks and I turn the podium over to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. McCloskey, before you proceed, risk management requires analysis, analysis of the past, talking about speed of speech. I think that I should - even before you have started - already ask you to have compassion with our transcriber and with our ears. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's nice to be remembered, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning. Srebrenica. Srebrenica has been a catastrophe for the Muslim community of Eastern Bosnia, a tragedy of such proportion that my words here today cannot begin to convey to you the suffering experienced by the people of Srebrenica. But the greatest tragedy is no longer found in the dead, for their suffering is over. We must also remember the families left behind, those people who have been condemned to live their lives without their fathers, without their husbands, their brothers, their sons, their neighbours, their community. There's too much pain, there's too much loss for any of us to truly comprehend the nature and scope of the shared misery of the women and survivors of the Srebrenica community. We can, however, strike back, as mandated by the Security Council with the creation of this Tribunal, to expose the horrific crimes of this war and try those most responsible for them. Through the comprehensive evidence presented in this case, we have revealed the nature and scope of this crime, this genocide. We have identified the key men responsible for it. We have Mladic in the dock answering for his crimes. The evidence of genocide presented in this courtroom for the last four and a half years - as promised in my opening - was clear, comprehensive, and unassailable. From the myriad of evidence presented, we see Mladic commanding his forces in an organised and systematic capture, detention, transportation, execution, and burial of over 7.000 able-bodied men and boys of Srebrenica and the expulsion of women and children and elderly actually on the ground in Potocari on film from 11 July throughout 13 July, Potocari, Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Nova Kasaba. For the next two sessions, I will take us back to 1995 and highlight for you the most important evidence proving Ratko Mladic's individual criminal responsibility and how that evidence has completely undone the Defence effort to deny it. In this case, the indictment has charged two related JCEs that pertain to Eastern Bosnia: The JCE to eliminate the Muslim population from Srebrenica; and the overarching JCE to ethnically cleanse the non-Serb population from Serb-controlled areas. I will focus my presentation on the JCE to eliminate, which - as you know - is defined as the forcible transfer of the women, children, and some elderly men of Srebrenica from 11 through 13 July, and the murder of the able-bodied men and boys of Srebrenica. In the months leading up to the fall of the enclave, the Srebrenica population had suffered systematic deprivation of food and other necessities of life, from deliberate restrictions of the aid to the population and supplies to UNPROFOR, to the planned assaults upon the civilian population, all resulting by 11 July in an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. These lasts words, as you know, are not mine. They are the words of Karadzic and Mladic as ordered in Directive 7 on 8 March 1995, P1469. I can think of no better description of the condition of the Srebrenica population on 11 July. Directive 7, when successfully turned into action, resulted in precisely what Mladic and Karadzic sought: A situation where the Muslim population, for their very survival, would have to leave Srebrenica. The women and children of Srebrenica were particularly vulnerable from 11 July because on that day the vast majority of their men were forced to flee their homes and families in fear for their lives. The Defence argue the population left voluntarily or were required to leave by UNPROFOR. However, by 11 July free will had been crushed by Mladic, replaced only with the will to survive. The hopeless condition of the population and the disabling of UNPROFOR were the result of Directive 7 and follow-up assaults, actions, and deprivations designed by Mladic and Karadzic to create this horrendous, inhuman situation for roughly 45.000 people in Srebrenica. The condition of the Muslim population on 11 July was a direct result of the policy of the VRS and Bosnian Serb leadership from the beginning of the war to remove non-Serbs, a policy that has been written down and spoken repeatedly by the Bosnian Serb leadership in official and unofficial documents, during meetings, and in private. Mr. Tieger and Mr. Traldi have reminded you of Strategic Objective 1 of May 1992, to separate the national communities; and Mladic's Directive 4 in November 1992, which ordered the removal of the Muslim population from the Srebrenica area. As you will recall from Mr. Traldi's presentation of that evidence, this is exactly what happened in early 1993, with the VRS successfully removing thousands of the people from Eastern Bosnia. However, the UN finally intervened in April 1993 with the creation of the protected areas through Security Council Resolution 819, which stalled further actions by the VRS. The intention to remove the Muslims from Srebrenica however remained and is clearly evident in the July 1994 report of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Ognjenovic, shortly after a meeting he had with Generals Mladic and Zivanovic known to you now and discussed previously by Mr. Tieger. These words - life has to be made unbearable - their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse, realising they cannot survive there. These words foreshadowing the criminal order in Directive 7 were, of course, not invented by Ognjenovic, but reflect what he learned from the meeting he had with Mladic and Zivanovic a few days earlier. We know this because some of the words on the same theme was noted down by General Zivanovic in his notebook. As Mr. Tieger pointed out, clear evidence that Ognjenovic based his report to his troops on the words of General Mladic and the discussion and the meeting he'd had. That's P5273. The enclave not so that they survive but so they disappear. And then in August 1994, we have Mladic's comments on videotape played to you by Mr. Tieger, where Mladic not only revelled in the destruction of Muslim homes, but exclaimed: "If the Americans and English, the Ukrainians, and the Canadians in Srebrenica - in the meantime it's the Dutch - would not protect them, they would have disappeared from this area long ago." Again, we see the use of the word "disappear," as we saw in Zivanovic's notes, a word Mladic will use again and again, revealing his intentions towards the Muslim community. Mladic's statement here reflects his frustrations with the UN enclaves and the international forces there, which prevented him from removing the Muslims from the area altogether at a time when he was yet unwilling to attack the UN forces. With the spring of 1995, we have Directive 7, on 8 March 1995. The same day Directive 7 was issued, Zivanovic had a meeting with Mladic and again made notes about Srebrenica, P5274. "Make life impossible." These words, of course, echo the theme of Directive 7 and are Mladic's words, as expressed by Miletic in Directive 7 or words to that effect. In addition to the order to complete unbearable conditions creating no hope of survival, Directive 7 sets out, as I mention, an insidious order to restrict aid to the enclaves, obviously in furtherance to create unbearable conditions. "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while, at the same time, avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." And, of course, this order in Directive 7 was followed and implemented, in many cases by Mladic himself who personally reviewed the convoy requests and initialled his decision to refuse crucially needed supplies. In one example found in P1788, page 16, Mladic denied an UNPROFOR request for fuel on 30 March, initialling the request with a big "no" on the top. Obradovic identified for us Mladic's initials here on transcript 14537 to 38. By carefully examining the rest of the exhibit, as well as Exhibits P2145, P2159, and P2146, you will see Mladic personally restricting materials and troops to UNPROFOR approximately 29 times. The Main Staff effort in restricting material to the enclaves is also evident from General Miletic's correspondence to the corps and brigades, instructing them regarding various restrictions. See paragraphs 435 to 447 of our brief. The next significant document recording the objective to remove the Muslims from Srebrenica is Mladic's order of 12 May 1995, instructing the Drina Corps to prepare battle plans against Zepa and Srebrenica. That's Exhibit P2097. However, on 16 May General Krstic informed the Main Staff in P2098 that while he was making preparation to follow Mladic's order, he states and I quote: "We are currently unable to implement your order to fully close off the enclaves and carry out attacks against them because we do not have sufficient forces ..." So unable to muster the troops available in May, the Drina Corps plans and conducts a successful sabotage action in June designed to instill fear and panic in the Srebrenica population. You will recall a small unit of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and Bratunac Brigade soldiers who secretly entered Srebrenica through a tunnel and fired several hand-held rockets in the fog towards the town. They also killed a woman they came across outside the tunnel. See our brief at paragraph 449. Milorad Pelemis, the commander of the unit, testified about this and tried to say that they were aiming at a police station with their RPGs, transcript 33812. I trust you will recall his incredible testimony in Pelemisi and the mass graves of 1992 which I will not get into. Needless to say, his testimony was not credible and the actual successful, objective of the attack was set out in his notes that we amazingly had, P7272. Coming into town and causing panic and disarray. This operation designed to instill fear and panic is perfectly consistent with Directive 7's objective, to make life unbearable. Next, later that month, the Drina Corps planned and executed a combat operation against DutchBat OP at Zeleni Jadar, removing that OP and paving the way for future assaults on Srebrenica from that area. This evidence is set out fully in our brief in paragraph 1107 and is based principally on VRS documents and DutchBat reports. So now on July 2nd the Drina Corps prepares an attack plan on the enclave itself, which I would like to show you and discuss briefly. It is P1465. First we can see that the attack plan is based on Directive 7 and 7/1. This, of course, totally undercuts the defence that Mladic withdrew the criminal order of Directive 7, replacing it with 7/1. This defence was thoroughly demolished by Mr. Tieger on Monday at transcript pages 44335 through 44336 and in our closing brief at paragraph 432. In addition, I refer you to Mr. Groome's questioning of General Milovanovic on this point, exposing the falsehoods underlying this defence document by document, question by question. In particular, see transcript pages 17123 to 17132. We see here the attack plan to divide Srebrenica and Zepa as I've mentioned to you before, a legitimate objective against the ABiH efforts to join the enclaves militarily and the order to reduce the enclaves to their urban areas, which, as we have shown, was designed to drive the civilian population from the rural parts of the enclave into the tiny urban area of Srebrenica, creating a humanitarian disaster like 1993. This, of course, was anything but legal. All thus, and I quote, "creating conditions for the elimination of the enclaves," which in this document meant creating the situation that would allow for the attack to now include taking the entire enclave and the removal of the population. This reference to elimination in the attack plan should not be confused with our use of the term "eliminate" in the JCE to eliminate. In the JCE to eliminate, we are referring to both the removal of the population and the murder of the able-bodied men, the murder to reveal itself a few days later. Accompanying the Krivaja 95 attack order was the operations map for the attack which shows Mladic's signature approving that order, P1087, page 25. The Defence suggests that Mladic approved the operation after the fact; however, there is no evidence of this whatsoever, and it makes no military sense for Mladic to approve such a critical operation post facto. The attack plan has also been sent to the Main Staff when it was issued on 2 July, of course. The next key document implementing the eventual removal of the population is the 9 July communique from Tolimir to Gvero and Krstic at the Pribicevac IKM, passing on Karadzic's approval to change the long-held strategy to create conditions for the elimination of the enclave to actually taking the entire enclave and expelling the Muslims. The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica. This document reflects Karadzic's approval of Mladic's proposal to take the entire enclave. This is the chain of command in action. While Mladic is not mentioned in this document, no one else was authorised to make such an important proposal to Karadzic, a proposal changing the two-year policy from creating conditions for the fall of the enclave to actually taking it, with a specific purpose of conquering the enclave and removing the population. The next day, the 10th of July, Mladic issued an order - based on the successes of 9 July - to begin preparations for the attack on Zepa, P2106. This document shows that Mladic had been fully informed of the events of 9 July and the crucial decision that was made. These are some of the amazing documents that form the historical record identifying the objective and intent behind the crime to remove the Muslim population from Srebrenica and setting the scene for the murder of the Srebrenica men and boys. With these documents, of course, the actions on the ground implementing them in furtherance of the criminal objective - to expel the Muslim population - occurred. After the delivery of Directive 7 to the Drina Corps, we see direct evidence of extreme convoy restrictions on DutchBat and the population; in short, DutchBat was barely able to function. This is described in detail by several Dutch witnesses and set out in our closing brief in paragraphs 435 to 447. The deprivations of the civilian population were so extreme, people were starving and beyond hope. See paragraphs 445 and 446 of our brief. Creating unbearable conditions was also accomplished by VRS attacks on the civilian population with the attack beginning 6 July as explained in detail in our brief. These assaults as planned by the VRS resulted in the movement of the population from the rural parts of the enclave, including the Swedish shelter project of roughly 3.000 inhabitants, into the urban area of Srebrenica, reaching critical mass on 10 and 11 July when the population surrounded the DutchBat base in Srebrenica known as the Bravo compound. You will recall the testimony of DutchBat witnesses Rave and Boering, describing how they were present the morning of 11 July when the VRS dropped a shell right in the middle of that crowd. We can only imagine the carnage that created. I want to show you one short clip to help remind us of the unbearable situation created by Karadzic and Mladic on 11 July in Srebrenica town. The images show the situation on 11 July, as Muslim civilians gather in total panic at the Bravo company compound, desperately trying to climb on UN vehicles to safety to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those images speak for themselves. As the terrified crowd fled Srebrenica towards Potocari, Rave described shells falling on both sides of the road all around the fleeing people, in what he thought was an effort to herd the people northward. You see that on transcript page 10171. By the evening of 11 July, the population was completely displaced from their homes, in terrible condition, many with babies and young children, without their men, with no means to survive for more than a few days at the most. Flight was their only option, as DutchBat had neither the manpower, facilities, or supplies to keep them alive and NATO air power proved worthless as the VRS now had several Dutch hostages. That evening, in his first meeting with Mladic, DutchBat Commander Karremans acknowledged the enclave was lost and requested Mladic's permission to allow DutchBat to leave along with the Muslim population. You will hear more about that later. That night Mladic personally ordered buses for their removal, which we know as you may remember from General Skrbic when he testified, transcript pages 13984 to 13985. Mladic was present in Potocari on the 12th and 13th, commanding his troops as they separated men and boys from their families, moved the women and children towards Kladanj, placed the men in detention prior to summary execution. The testimony and video accounts of these two horrific days have exposed this expulsion. The fear is palpable on the faces of Muslims caught on video. Nothing put forward by the Defence has undercut this in any way, shape, or form. I want to show you a video from our Srebrenica trial video that shows the massive numbers of people in Potocari on 12 July. And if you look carefully, you'll see the many able-bodied men scattered throughout, the same men the Bosnian Serbs would have seen the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wish I could bring you the heat and the smells and the sweat and everything that you can imagine that the -- the horror that that must have been. The idea that these people voluntarily left is insulting. Next, also from our trial video, we have a clip where you will see women, children, and elderly actually being expelled and forced to walk across the front lines, 5 kilometres in 35-degree heat, towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The subtitling was a little hard to read, but the last woman said: "What am I going to do? I have four children. I'm left to suffer with them." And then: "How can we ... how are we supposed to live now? " We have seen the documents underlying this crime of forcible transfer and recalled the conduct of Mladic's forces implementing the policy and the orders for expulsion. However, that's not all that you have seen in this courtroom. I'm sure you remember we have Mladic's own words ordering the expulsion of the population. On 12 July, Mladic gets on the radio and it gets intercepted. I'll show you the transcript. "Mladic: Have these buses and trucks left? "Mladic: Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They have all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all -- those who want to and those who don't want to." That's at P1235. Lastly, you heard a tape-recording of Mladic, where sometime after the war Mladic is bragging about how he accomplished his victory over the Srebrenica people. I won't play that today, but let's read what he said. "I would not have taken Srebrenica or Zepa, if I had not starved them in the winter, since February, I let through only one or two convoys." You remember when I played that tape for General Obradovic and he had the integrity to identify Mladic's voice and thus authenticate the tape. The evidence is unambiguous and undeniable. The Muslim population of Srebrenica was expelled on 11 through 13 July by Mladic and his forces, acting under the long-time policy and orders to remove them. Mladic gave the population no choice: For their very survival, they had to leave Srebrenica. That would be a good time, I think, to take the break before I go to the murder operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are -- I leave it in your hands. I mean, there's some flexibility. We are five minutes off from one hour, but if you think this would be a better moment, there is no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will take a break. We will resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. The murder operation. The summary execution of over 7.000 Muslim men and boys and the operation to expel the women and children 11 to 13 July were fundamentally one major undertaking, with two interconnected operations, what I refer to as the forcible transfer operation and the murder operation, both designed to dispose the entire Srebrenica population, which we have defined in the indictment as the JCE to eliminate. Now, we speak about these operations separately, but - as you know from all the evidence - they are so intertwined and together, especially on the 12th and 13th of July that they must be viewed as one. That is the foundation of the JCE to eliminate. For the purpose of my argument today, I've divided the Prosecution case into four chapters: The first, the mass executions of over 7.000 able-bodied men from 13 through 23 July and beyond; the second, the evidence identifying the perpetrators of these crimes, exclusively VRS and MUP officers acting under the command of Ratko Mladic; and third, the presence, conduct, and actions of General Mladic from 11 July through 17 July, commanding the units both from the ground and from Belgrade. These three chapters themselves form the foundation of proving Mladic's criminal responsibility but there's more, and what is largely part of chapter 3, I call chapter 4. It's where I take you through some of the most compelling evidence specifically identifying Mladic's involvement in the planning, ordering, and overseeing the mass murders. The Defence appear to acknowledge, to some degree, that large-scale murders occurred during the key time-frame. They, however, suggest that our murder victims' numbers are inflated, that they are battle casualties in the mass graves, but for the most part there is no serious defence challenging the mass murders. The Defence agree with the Prosecution to some extent that Beara and Popovic and other security officers were significantly involved in those murders. They seem to suggest in their closing brief that Krstic was also involved, which we agree. Krstic played a major role in these crimes. Also, I understand the Defence fundamentally agree with the Prosecution regarding Mladic's whereabouts from 11 July through the evening of 6 [sic] July and I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 6 July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To the evening of 16th July, excuse me. And I believe they agree that Mladic was on duty in Bosnia on 11 July through the afternoon of 14 July, when he crossed over the border into Serbia. However, the Defence impossibly leave Mladic and his troops out of the crimes, arguing that he had no knowledge and no involvement in the mass murders and neither did his VRS or police forces, except for a few security officers. Thus, the most significant issues of disagreement are the identities of the perpetrators of the murder operation and Mladic's command of the murder operation and his links and connection to it. The Defence military expert concluded the murders were committed by, and I quote: "Self-organised paramilitary groups from Podrinje coming from pre-was criminal milieus, as well as by groups of avengers ... probably committed in co-operation with some officers from security structures." That's D1661, page 232 and with no other involvement from the VRS or MUP forces under Mladic's command, despite our prodding on cross-examination of: Who are these people? Who did it? And that, despite being on duty in and around the places where the crimes were committed, Mladic was unaware and uninvolved in any of these forces and the crimes they supposedly committed. So first the mass executions. The evidence of the crimes is overwhelming. It came to you first-hand in most cases from the survivors themselves and in many cases executioners who shared the same ground as those they murdered. This was backed up by forensic crime scene investigation, aerial imagery, vehicle records, witnesses, exhumations of all the known mass graves from Srebrenica connecting all the primary graves -- primary disturbed mass graves to all the secondary graves. As of today, we have identified almost 6.000 murder victims from mass graves; and with so many people still missing, we expect the final number of murdered is over 7.000 people. I saw no significant Defence challenge to our major executions and mass grave evidence, as I mentioned, challenging only the Jadar River and Cerska executions, the murder of the Milici patients, and arguing the Kravica mass murders were merely revenge-based on killing of a MUP soldier by a Muslim prisoner. I will rely on our brief for the detailed analysis of those cases, but I do want to remind you of some of the key points. You will remember the evidence of the Jadar River murders. We've spent a fair amount of time with them and the witnesses and in the 98 bis arguments. I thus refer to you our closing brief paragraphs 1426 to 1435. But remember the survivor RM314, his testimony, his demeanour, all the corroborating and supporting evidence where he was captured, taken to a river, shot, fell in the river, washed downstream, and escaped. The Defence twists the meaning of the Latin term used in his medical report, the term "vulna explosiva." They try to argue that it means it's a shrapnel wound; however, the evidence at trial has clearly shown that that's not the case. The term describes the victim's wound and does not refer to the cause of the wound. We hear that from the doctors in their reports. Regarding Cerska, the murder of 150 men from Srebrenica, though we don't have a survivor of that execution, the witnesses, forensic evidence, and evidence of the 17 July sweep operation ordered by Mladic to Keserovic proves that the 150 Muslims captured in the sweep operation on 17 July were executed at Cerska on 17 or 18 July. See our brief at paragraphs 1341 to 1347 and 1540 to 1545. The crux of the Cerska issue lies in determining the date Keserovic received the order from Mladic to conduct the sweep operation. We've proven that Mladic gave Keserovic this order on the night of 16 July, after Mladic returned from Belgrade; as such, the murders of the 150 victims at Cerska was the direct result of Mladic's order. While Keserovic resisted confirming his previous testimony that he received the order on 16 July, he did not waiver from his account that he received that order personally from Mladic the night before he departed to Bratunac. We have proven Keserovic travelled to Bratunac on the 17th of July, thus proving he received the order from Mladic in Crna Rijeka the night of the 16th, all of which ties Mladic directly to the murders at Cerska. Remember the young boy that was gathered up in the sweep operation on the 17th. He identified people he knew that were later found among the 150 at Cerska, and those people were killed as a result of the order of the sweep operation, which happened right in the centre of the murder operation time-period. As for Kravica, this is a complex situation with several different forms of interlocking evidence. You remember the mass murder of some 800 to 1.000 people in the Kravica warehouse not long after Mladic had left the Sandici meadow, maybe an hour or two. The evidence is from survivors, MUP witnesses, video, video transcripts, a careful re-creation by Mr. Blaszczyk, and more. We have thoroughly analysed this and due to its complexity I can't get into it with you today, but please take a look at the break -- at the brief. I do want you to consider two or three things, though. You should note that both the Defence and the Prosecution appear to agree that a Muslim prisoner took a rifle from a MUP guard and killed him, whereupon another MUP soldier grabbed the barrel of the Muslim's rifle, burning his hands as he took it away. The basic difference is that the Defence argue that the shooting of the MUP soldier started the killing spree, whereas it's the Prosecution's case that this incident was an organised execution pursuant to orders, with the burned hands incident happening well after the executions had begun and it was a desperate response by a Muslim man to the executions around him, not how they started. So the key to unlocking Kravica is understand the evidence that shows burned hands could only have happened around the east side of the warehouse, many minutes after the killings started at the west side of the warehouse. This can been seen from evaluating the two survivor witnesses, RM256, who was in the west room; and RM274 who was in the east room and a careful review of the video of Borovcanin arriving at the scene, remembering he wasn't too far away when he hurried there straight after getting the report about burned hands. Now, like all survivors in this situation, their accounts have differences, but the similarities and connections are much stronger than those few differences; and when combined with all the evidence, it's obvious that burned hands did not start this execution. For our analysis of the murders of the Milici patients, please refer to our brief 1375 to 1378, where we carefully explain the evidence that shows Popovic removed ten seriously injured Muslims from the Zvornik Brigade on 23 July and they have never been seen since. And we had their names and their medical documents clearly identifying who those people are. There's no question that once Popovic had them in his hands on the 23rd, the man that authored the Bisina executions that same day, that they were taken out and killed. Back to the overall case. As I said, aside from the crimes I've just mentioned above, the Defence and their experts have not significantly challenged the major execution sites, as far as I can tell - perhaps we'll hear something new next week - suggesting only that some of the people exhumed from the mass graves were battle casualties. There is, in fact, no evidence that anyone but murder victims were placed in the graves at Branjevo Farm, Kozluk, Petkovci Dam, Orahovac, and all the secondary graves coming from those enormous graves. Only the grave at Glogova contained the victims who died in unknown circumstances, such as combat, murder, or other means that we don't know about. As you know, Glogova was used, it was along the road, and it is impossible to know how many bodies were along that road and died in ways that we don't know. We do know that Glogova contained all the bodies of the 800 to some 1.000 murder victims from Kravica warehouse and those murdered in the schools in Bratunac - well, over 50, though the precise numbers in the circumstances, as I mentioned, are impossible to determine. We did our best in the brief to lay this out for you. So not only is there no evidence supporting the Defence claim of battle casualties in the graves, there is really no reason whatsoever the VRS would have used the valuable men and resources to undertake such a project. The areas of conflict were remote, densely wooded, largely inaccessible areas which, of course, reflects the route the column took to avoid Serb forces. Bodies in these remote areas posed no significant threat or health hazard worth risking men and materials for. The woods were not only dense and inaccessible but contained desperate Muslims trapped there after the fall of Srebrenica, some of them were armed, there were also mines in those woods. There was a terrible threat for anyone going there. Finally, the mass graves were far away from the conflict area. Orahovac was the closest, some 5 kilometres but even then the terrain was very difficult. There is no reason on earth you would go look for harmless bodies and pull them with masses -- trucks and resources all the way out to these places. I won't show you the map. You know the places, the distance. It's absurd. This defence is unsupported, completely unreasonable, and should be rejected. Okay, Chapter 2, the forces committing these crimes. Throughout the Srebrenica section of their brief, the Defence conclude Colonel Beara, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Momir Nikolic, and Drago Nikolic played major roles in organising and implementing the murder operation. On this point, we fundamentally agree. However, after somewhat acknowledging Beara's and Popovic's involvement, the Defence goes completely off the rails and state that the murders, as I had said, were not conducted by Mladic's forces but self-organised paramilitary groups and groups of avengers whose family members had been killed. These words from the expert Kovac are more words of desperation and defensiveness than anything resembling credible evidence or argument. There is no evidence whatsoever that people resembling this description played any role in the murder operation or were even present in the area. When asked in cross-examination to identify such a group, Kovac could only identify the Skorpions. That's at transcript 41855. However, remember how much time we spent with the material there. You have seen the VRS documents, map graphics, and other evidence showing the Skorpions were a Serbian MUP unit engaged in combat in the SRK zone of responsibility, resubordinated to the VRS and under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. There's a key document and its number has escaped me in my brief, but I remember Dragomir Milosevic says "our forces" in the top of it and he lists the wounding of Skorpions. I think some even were killed that day in July. That is in our brief. And the Skorpions, I'm not going to show you that awful video, but please take care here. Sometimes because that video is so clear and the Muslims are so obviously from Srebrenica, we have not laid out the facts and the details of that crime as much as we should have. We have now.
