But this needs to be done to fully understand that this was part of the murder operation, part of the JCE to eliminate. The evidence of the actual officers, units, and troops taking part in the murder operation from 13 July onwards is clearly set out in our closing brief, so I'm going to summarise for you here and even that gets a little tedious because there are so many VRS people, but I need to remind you of them. In and around Potocari commanding the forces were Mladic, Krstic, Borovcanin, with Popovic, Momir Nikolic, Petar Salapura, Radoslav Jankovic, Kosoric implementing the operation, using soldiers and officers of the Bratunac Brigade including military police, RS MUP, special police officers of the 65th Protection Regiment, members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and others. In Bratunac from 11 through 13 July, Mladic was present, together with Krstic, Zivanovic, Popovic, Borovcanin, Radislav Jankovic, and all of the Drina Corps brigade commanders taking part in the attack on Srebrenica, including Pandurevic, Blagojevic, Furtula, Trivic, and others. In the Zvornik area, deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Dragan Obrenovic, played a key role in the events, as did Vinko Pandurevic when he returned from the Zepa battle on 15 July. The brigade duty officers from 14 through 17 July were heavily involved in organising the executions with the commands of the 4th Battalion in Orahovac, the 6th Battalion in Petkovci, the 2nd Battalion in Rocevic, and the 1st Battalion in Pilica, the officers, soldiers, and units involved in the Zvornik-area murders are too numerous to name here. The Defence failure to acknowledge this enormous body of evidence of direct VRS and MUP involvement highlight how desperate and unreasonable the Defence case truly is. Perhaps they will come up with something that we'll hear next week. Okay, Chapter 3. The presence of Mladic in and around Srebrenica Bratunac and Zvornik areas at various times between 11 July and the afternoon of 14 July is not contested by the Defence. The evidence is, of course, overwhelming from witnesses, documents, intercepts, and especially video of Mladic in Srebrenica on the 11th of July, at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th and 12th of July, and in Potocari on the 12th of July to name some of the sources. All of this evidence clearly shows Mladic in uniform, on duty, in command, exercising command. The idea that Krstic was in command was thoroughly debunked by Mr. Tieger and I won't go over that in specifics. The Defence suggest in their brief at paragraph 643, when present at the corps command post, Mladic could only offer advice to corps commander and could not overrule the corps commander's authority. That's what Mr. Tieger was speaking to when he debunked it and outlined well how the chain of command worked and Mladic's role into it. I won't go any further into it. So Chapter 4. And now this takes me to the evidence linking Mladic to the creation, ordering, and implementation of the murder operation. We begin, as we have before, with Mladic's now-famous words uttered at about 5.30 p.m. on 11 July during his walk through Srebrenica town. This is P1147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "The time has come to take revenge upon the Turks in this region." These words must be taken seriously, for within six days of their utterance Mladic's officers and men murdered over 7.000 Muslim able-bodied men and boys. Now let's go to the evening of 11 July and the first meeting with the DutchBat at the Hotel Fontana. I want to draw your attention to significant moments at the Hotel Fontana that should help reveal Mladic's intentions and strategies and his decision to murder the able-bodied men of Srebrenica on the evening of 11 July or the morning of 12 July. During the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana on 11 July, Mladic intimidated Karremans and his officers and threatened them with references to death and other vulgarities. You've seen that. I won't play that for you again. Previously, we've asked you to consider this evidence to show that there was no negotiation at the Hotel Fontana and that Mladic was in complete control, intimidating everyone. This remains the case, but I would also like to focus you this time on the words of Colonel Karremans in response to Mladic. So after screaming and threatening the Dutch officers, Mladic finally and deliberately calms down and asks Karremans, and I quote: "What do you want? You asked for the meeting! Speak up." This is – I’ll show you the transcript of what the colonel said. "I had a talk with General Nikolai two hours ago ... and also with the national authorities about the request on behalf of the population. It's a request because I'm not in a position to demand anything. We ... the command in Sarajevo has said that the enclave has been lost." He goes on to say: "And the request of the BH command is to ... let's say, to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion and the withdrawal of those refugees and if there are possibilities to assist that withdrawal." That's from our trial video, P1147, transcript page 17. As you can see, Karremans tells Mladic that the UN command has concluded that the enclave has been lost and he requested Mladic's approval for the withdrawal of DutchBat and thousands of refugees in Potocari. Well, this is what I call a water-shed moment for Mladic and Karadzic, after years of efforts to remove the Muslims from Eastern Bosnia, only to be prevented in 1993 through 11 July by UNPROFOR, but now UNPROFOR has given up and is requesting Mladic to allow them and the Muslim population to leave Srebrenica. Of course, Mladic has not given UNPROFOR any real choice. He had thousands of Muslim hostages, Dutch hostages, Muslims struggling to survive, no longer any military option and no NATO. But the point I want to make to you is: With the complete surrender, Mladic is now able to focus his decision-making and resources on removing the population and dealing with the able-bodied men in Potocari and elsewhere in the enclave. We know from Mladic's Main Staff assistant commander for personnel, Skrbic, as I mentioned, that Mladic himself ordered buses late that night. Skrbic testified about this, 13984 to 13985. Also that evening, Mladic ordered Borovcanin to make the final assault on Potocari first thing in the morning of 12 July. See Borovcanin's report, P72 [sic]. And as you will recall -- P724, excuse me. As you will recall, Borovcanin and elements of the Bratunac Brigade did make an unopposed assault on Potocari the morning of the 12th and soon controlled the Muslim population. So with no obstacles from the UN or NATO on the evening of July, Mladic can now look squarely at the able-bodied men that he knows are in his -- that will soon be in his control. You recall the evidence. The VRS had observed those men the night of the 11th and reported it to Mladic. See paragraph 1159 of our brief. At the second Hotel Fontana meeting with a Muslim school teacher, Nesib Mandzic, we see Mladic now focus on the Bosnian army, repeatedly insisting on meeting the next day with a representative of the Muslim army. After that meeting, Mladic and Krstic had dinner together at the Hotel Fontana where they were both staying. See paragraphs 1174 and 1219 of our brief. Mladic's intel officers Jankovic and Kosoric were also seen on the video at the hotel. So this is decision-making time. In the quiet, comfortable surroundings of a hotel at the end of the day with his key people to advise him, the Muslims of Potocari had to be the main focus of discussion. Mladic had ordered the buses that night to remove the population. And his other major -- immediate decision was what to do with the able-bodied men who would be in his control the next day. The next morning, at the third Hotel Fontana meeting, Mladic announced his decision to screen the able-bodied men in Potocari from 16 to 60, thus we know he made his decision between the late evening of 11 and the morning of 12 July he had made a decision about those able-bodied men, to screen them. We know that from his announcement. Next, you will recall the testimony of Momir Nikolic, explaining how that morning, before the Hotel Fontana meeting, Popovic and Kosoric approached him and informed him that all the able-bodied men would be killed and they needed his assistance. See paragraph 1176 of our brief and his testimony at 11820 and 11827. Thus, the decision Mladic had made to screen the men in Potocari was, in fact, the decision to separate and murder them. This soon became evident when the separations began. There was never any significant screening of the men. There was a rough and sometimes violent division of males from the population, including many times boys 13 to 15 and younger and older men well over 60. The men were crowded together in inhuman conditions, in extreme heat, with no food or medicine, and only enough water to sustain them. Identification documents were discarded and burned in the process, showing Mladic had no concern for these people as prisoners of war and wanted no record of who they were. You may recall the photos of a large pile of Muslim belongings, including IDs, being burned in Potocari after 13 July. That's Exhibit P1423. In their detention in nearby Bratunac, the separated men were routinely beaten and many were killed by the troops guarding them. The separations and detentions in Potocari and Bratunac confirm Mladic's decision to screen the men was actually a decision to murder them. Before I go any further I want to play to you Mladic's words at the second Hotel Fontana meeting because, again, I think his words give away his intent. This is to Nesib Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Destruction, salvation, fear. Mr. Tieger has already played for you part of the 12 July meeting where we see similar words. I won't do that again, but I will remind you of what those words ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- is there any interpretation problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is, let's check whether ... I'll speak a few words again. Nothing yet. I see that some action was taken. I don't know whether it resolves it. It does. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what you should be seeing on the screen is the transcript of the video Mr. Tieger showed you on Monday. "There is no need for your people to get killed ... your husband, your brothers, or your neighbours ... as I have told this gentleman last night, you can either survive or disappear. For your survival, I demand that all your armed men, even those who committed crimes - and many did - against our people, surrender their weapons to the VRS." Again, survive, disappear. Given the next -- what Mladic and his troops did the next few days, these words have to be taken deadly seriously. The Muslim man Mladic was speaking to on this video is Ibro Nuhanovic. After this meeting, he stayed with his adult son Muhamed and his wife Nasiha, all of whom were murdered. Their remains have been recovered. See P1982 and paragraph 1197 of our final brief. Also remember the evidence in this case that the commander of the Zepa Brigade, Avdo Palic, was also murdered in the custody of the VRS. Throughout the day on 12 July, Mladic oversaw the horrendous separation process going on in Potocari, making propaganda films for his public, and falsely comforting the people with hollow promises and outright lies. On the evening of 12 July, Mladic held a meeting and dinner at the Bratunac Brigade HQ to celebrate the taking of the enclave. During this meeting, Mladic announced the assembled troops would move to Zepa the following morning, 13 July, against the advice - if you recall - of Commanders Pandurevic and Trivic, and ordered Krstic to prepare an attack plan for the next day. This is a classic example of Mladic exercising command and control over his subordinate commanders, as Krstic duly drafted the plan, D290; and the assembled Drina Corps troops did March to Zepa area the next day as ordered, even though that left Zvornik undefended, where a few days later many, many Serb soldiers were killed when the Muslim column and the forces of the 2nd Corps met them on the 16th of July. The Defence argues this meeting took place on 11 July but that is absolutely wrong, and the evidence clearly establishes the dinner meeting was held on the evening of 12 July. We cover this evidence thoroughly in our brief at paragraphs 1215 to 1226, conclusively proving that this meeting occurred on the evening of 12 July. This is an important historical meeting and a key to understanding the sequence of events. On the evening of 11 July, Mladic and Krstic were together at the Hotel Fontana for dinner after their meetings with DutchBat, as we've discussed, where the fate of the Muslim men was decided. On the 12 July, Mladic is at the meeting with the brigade commanders to celebrate where the decision is made to go to Zepa. 13 July. The events of 13 July, more than any other day, expose the depth of Mladic's involvement in the murder operation. The 13th is the climax of the expulsions, where the final push is made to transport thousands of remaining women and children towards Zepa [sic] while continuing the separations of hundreds of able-bodied men in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, towards Kladanj and not towards Zepa. This is an enormous undertaking, thus Mladic is there in the area most of the day overseeing this work. He is right in the middle of this. Bratunac in the morning at meetings, a trip near Srebrenica to inspire the troops, and then back to Potocari where the separations and expulsions continue. Also that morning and through the rest of the day, Mladic and his people are totally swamped by the surrender and capture of roughly 6.000 Muslims from the column fleeing Srebrenica, and it is here dealing with these thousands of people where Mladic and his people get sloppy and begin to reveal the murder operation. The organised murders begin that morning, first seen by the investigation with the Jadar River executions at about 11.00 a.m. where - as I mention - the killers fail to kill RM314, who was washed down to safety to tell his story. Also, and this is very significant, Beara is first heard in an intercept speaking on an open line issuing orders organising the hundreds of Muslims who had been captured around Konjevic Polje. So Beara has now clearly been brought in to deal with these prisoners. At this time, Mladic is close by, down the road in Srebrenica or Bratunac. And remember, Beara's only work from 13 through 16 July was to implement the murder operation. Let me show you some of Beara's comments that morning in speaking to Lieutenant Lucic of the 65th Protection Regiment, Zoran Malinic's deputy. This is an intercept, Exhibit P1415. "Beara: Do you know that 400 balijas have shown up in Konjevic Polje? "And they have been rounded up disarmed, everything. "Beara: Excellent, excellent, great. "And there is someone to guard them. "Beara: Shove them all on the playground. "Who gives a fuck about them? "Beara: Well, line them up in four to five rows." Then Beara is told by Zoka, which is Malinic's nickname, that some of the Muslims are killing themselves and his response is: "Well, excellent. Just let them continue. Fuck it." The Defence agree Beara is involved in the murder operation. As I'd mentioned, Mladic is in the area with Krstic, Salapura, Popovic, Nikolic, and others, all able to provide him information. To suggest Mladic doesn't know Beara is involved or what he is doing is absolutely absurd. The next example of sloppy communication revealing the murder operation and Mladic's role in it comes from a Tolimir proposal drafted and sent to Mladic on the afternoon of 13 July by the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment, Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. The number of captured prisoners increased so dramatically that day that Tolimir got involved, even though he was in Rogatica and busy with the impending attack on the Zepa enclave. But the security breach - or sloppiness - appears to be Savcic's, as he is the one that actually drafted the Tolimir proposal. Now, we had spent a fair amount of time with this, so I – I’ll just make some conclusions for you. The document reveals that the top VRS commanders and staff are all involved with the many hundreds of Muslims captured along the road. We can see from the document the proposal is from Tolimir, it's to Mladic, copied to Gvero, and mentioning and involving Miletic, Malinic, and drafted by Savcic. Where Savcic gets sloppy is in item 3, where in referring to the Muslim prisoners in Nova Kasaba in this proposal is to put them out of sight from the ground and the air. At that time the international forces were the only ones with free access to the skies, thus this proposal is designed to hide the prisoners from NATO or UNPROFOR. This is a clear indication that the intention at the time was to kill the prisoners. Any doubt regarding their intent to kill in this document was dispelled by Savcic himself, the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you read "ground and the air," where the text you were reading states "ground or the air."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Savcic testified here and provided statements where he acknowledged that the proposal was meant to hide prisoners from NATO and was asked simply: Why? And he opined the reason for this was the VRS concern that NATO would mistake the Muslims for Serbs and bomb them. See transcript pages 33680-33682. That is so beyond absurd that it can only lead to the fair inference that he knew what the truth was and lied to our face. Now, let's see, I want to show you Mladic's response to Tolimir's proposal. This is Mladic's order, adopting Tolimir's proposal, written with much more discretion, failing to mention hiding prisoners from NATO, but you will recall that on the 13th all the prisoners were held either in vehicles or indoors, where they could not be seen from the air. By the evening of the 13th, there are up to 6.000 prisoners captured along the road and the decision is made to move them to Zvornik, away from the international organisations present in Bratunac and Potocari. You may recall that Karadzic is intercepted at 8.10 p.m. that night, telling Deronjic to make sure "goods" are in the warehouse by the next day, a reference to the prisoners in Bratunac being sent to schools around Zvornik. That intercept is at Exhibit P1290. Also that night, Drago Nikolic informed Major Obrenovic - deputy commander at the time - that Mladic and his superior commanders had ordered the murder of the Srebrenica prisoners and that Popovic needed Drago to help assist in the operation. That's in paragraph 1271 of our brief. In another proposal late that night, Tolimir proposes to Gvero at the Main Staff in a written document that 800 prisoners could be moved in secret to Rogatica to carry out agricultural work, maintaining a horse, pig, and a sheep farm. There was no work to maintain the farm according to Djoko Razdoljac, a Rogatica Brigade logistics officer whose testimony is part of this trial. Tolimir's proposal was P2121. At the same time, Tolimir, Karadzic, and many others are dealing with issues related to detaining, transporting, and killing prisoners. Beara is in Bratunac dealing with the prisoners held at the schools, with Bratunac Brigade MP lawyer Celanovic. He's also dealing with the transport to Zvornik of prisoners with Nikolic. And together with the civilian authorities, he's dealing with the burial of the hundreds and hundreds of victims from the Kravica warehouse. And finally, in the afternoon, Mladic travels the road where now thousands of prisoners are being held and he stops and gives speeches to them at Sandici meadow and Nova Kasaba. While there, Mladic has personally ordered Major Malinic, commander of the MP battalion there, to stop noting down names of prisoners and to escort the prisoners to Bratunac. Mladic again is trying to hide the prisoners. His specific involvement in stopping the list-taking is a critical piece of evidence for you and it's clearly established by Keserovic. Also, it's amazing Mladic has the -- he's so familiar with the details of this. He tells Malinic that buses will soon be arriving and they do, and he orders them to send them to Bratunac. See our brief at paragraphs 1260 to 1261. From there, Mladic travels on to the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica where he held a ceremony promoting Krstic to commander of the Drina Corps that evening. And remember everything that Beara is doing right down the road in Bratunac with the prisoners, the burials, the movements, prisoners actually got transported that night to Zvornik. I show you this document, the personnel document, showing Krstic's appointment to corps commander because we can see that it's pursuant to decree of the President of Republika Srpska. So we see that Karadzic and Mladic are together on this critical appointment. Of course, they are. They're within communications, it's a major decision. Again, this is the chain of command in action. This is Exhibit P7056. After this, Mladic went to his command post at Crna Rijeka where he spent the night, another place where the information is waiting for him; he can get everything he needs to know. So during all the activity I've outlined for you happening pursuant to the murder operation, Mladic is right there in the thick of it, with the masses of condemned prisoners, with his key officers at the command post, which are all communications hubs and sources of the latest intel. The Defence argues he knows nothing and is not involved. Absolutely unthinkable. Mladic is a criminal but he is no fool. I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we take the break, how much time would you need? You said two sessions. I think you used two sessions, and how much time would Mr. Tieger need after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I didn't use quite two sessions. Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Minus five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope I can get done in 20 or 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, how much would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No more than ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No more than ten minutes. That would then fit, if Mr. McCloskey sticks to his estimate, then that would still fit into the time we have available until a quarter past 2.00. We take a break and we'll resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if you take until 2.00, then Mr. Tieger has some time to go beyond his assessment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now we're at 14th of July. So Mladic he is at the Main Staff command on the morning of the 14th as the massive work pursuant to murder operation continues, most clearly in the enormous convoy and buses and trucks from Bratunac taking men to the schools in the Zvornik area, led by Popovic, men that would be killed at Orahovac that day, Petkovci that night, and onward. Mladic travels the same route as the convoy early in the afternoon of the 14th. As he is going by Zvornik, it's roughly the same time people are being murdered at Orahovac, not far away. It's inconceivable that Mladic's forces are engaged in this massive murder operation with him in the area and him not fully informed, involved, and in command. Mladic remained in command and control of the VRS while he was in Belgrade with no other officer standing in for him. I refer you to that, to our brief 1325 to 1327, but I'll remind you of the testimony of Colonel Obradovic, his chief of operation, who was asked by Mr. Lukic about the issue of Mladic's absence and standing in at transcript pages 14543 to 44. Mr. Lukic asked: "Would going to Serbia be considered absent." Colonel Obradovic answered, and I quote: "It doesn't depend on the whereabouts of the commander, but it depends on the duration of absence." The Trial Chamber then queried the witness on what time-period this would be, and Obradovic answered: "A week or so to my mind." As you know, even by the Defence count Mladic would only have been in Belgrade a bit more than three days. In any event, Mladic could have been in a coma from the late afternoon of the 14 July and he would have still been criminally responsible for his involvement in the developing and implementing the JCE to eliminate from 11 July through 14 July, and there's no real issue of alibi here. Finally, I would like to finish my discussion of the evidence with three intercepts, but first I want to tell you the story that these intercepts reveal and then we'll go over them. On the 13th of July when the massive numbers of Muslims were being captured along the road and Beara was so involved, he needed help to execute people and he received an order from Mladic to brigade commander of the Visegrad Brigade, Radomir Furtula. Mladic ordered Furtula to provide him with 30 men from his unit to assist Beara. That day the men were loaded on a bus in Visegrad, headed up, and soon after that their bus broke down. And by the evening of 13 July they still hadn't been retrieved and nobody knows what they did after that, but Beara never got them. So by 15 July, after the men in Orahovac had been killed, the men in Petkovci had been killed, there were still over 800 men needing to be killed at Kozluk, at the Rocevic school, and over 1700 [Realtime transcript read in error "17"] people that are backed up at the Pilica school and the Pilica Dom. And as you will remember, the Muslim column is now approaching Zvornik and is a real threat to Zvornik. Vinko Pandurevic gets called back to help defend Zvornik. Other troops are going in to fight the column. At the same time, the murder operation is occurring taking tremendous resources and Beara is very frustrated. He has got all of these well over 2.000 people that he needs to kill and he is pulling his hair out. So he gets on the phone looking for Zivanovic who he thinks is still the corps commander. He is calling from Drago Nikolic's office at the Zvornik Brigade. Zivanovic tells him he can't do that anymore and he refers him to Krstic's extension, 385. And Beara gets on the line with Krstic and says the same thing he said to Zivanovic, that Furtula did not follow the boss's order, referring the boss is to be Mladic, as Zivanovic had referred to him before. They go back and forth and back and forth. Krstic tells him to check with various brigade commanders, the Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, Milici Brigade. Beara says, no, they won't do it, they can't do it. He says, Well, talk to those guys at the MUP. They can't do it either and they are very frustrated. Finally it ends with Beara saying, Look, I have 3500 parcels to deliver and I have no solution. These are the men in Kozluk and the men in Pilica. Krstic ends it with: "Well, now I'm going to be the one to blame" - worried about being blamed by Mladic - and says: "I'll see what I can do." The next day, 16 July, the Main Staff 10th Sabotage Unit comes and assists at Branjevo Farm. That was the information fundamentally provided by Mr. Butler in some of the evidence, but let's now take a look at the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do, can you please look at page 65, line 16, and the number 17 there; is that what you had said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, when I said over 800 men needing to be killed, I was speaking in the context of Beara, who felt he needed to kill --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 800 is there. Look at "17."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, it should be 1700.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I thought I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you'll recall that number from the number of people exhumed from the Branjevo Farm mass grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the slide of the first -- this is just a short reference that shows that at 9.52 hours Beara is looking for Zivanovic and wants him to call him at 139. 139 is Drago Nikolic's extension at the Zvornik Brigade and there's other evidence that that's where Beara is at the time. So let's go to the next slide. I won't go over all of it, but you can see Beara saying: "You know that day, I informed the commander about it, Furtula didn't send Lukic's intervention platoon." Furtula, that's Dragomir Furtula, the commander of the Visegrad Brigade. Lukic is Milan Lukic, an infamous person from Visegrad, and Lukic is waiting at Blagojevic's. That would be Blagojevic of the Bratunac Brigade. Beara says: "Lukic is here with me and his driver and we urged that." A bit more complaining about Furtula and then Beara says: "He simply doesn't give a damn about what the commander ordered him to do. Well, now, that platoon has 60 men." That is it a reference to Mladic's order to Furtula to give Beara 60 men. And then Beara goes down and says: "Have him send me at least half." And then finally Zivanovic says: "I can't decide that anymore. Now you remember, this is 15 July. Zivanovic was removed from commander on the night of the 13th July, so he can't make decisions for Beara anymore. And also this is a -- fundamentally exposes the appropriate and proper chain of command, not like anything else. This is a Main Staff security officer. He is having to go to the corps commander to get the corps commander to issue orders to his brigades. Beara, the colonel, can't do it himself; the commander is the one that's in charge. This idea that Mladic is out of the loop and that the security branch can run the whole show is absurd. So finally at the end we see that Zivanovic refers him to 385, Zlatar that's the Drina Corps extension, and to ask for 385. We know from other evidence that that's where Krstic can be reached. Okay. So now let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said have him sent at least half you added the word "me" whether it makes any difference, but if you quote, if you read literally, I would like you to do that very precisely. At least that's what I heard you say. Sent me, that's what you said, whereas the text says let him send -- It may be the same. I'm just -- if you read --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm working in my argument throughout this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and I don't mean to be -- to mislead you like that. What I think he meant by that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So now naturally we see him, Beara, get connected to Krstic. So let's go to the next, which is P2126. And this is at 1000 hours on the 15th. And Beara tells Krstic: "General Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order. Again, this is referring to Mladic's order to Furtula. Krstic says: "Listen, he ordered him to lead out a tank not a train." This is an indication Krstic is fully aware of Mladic's order to Furtula. It appears that Krstic is making a veiled reference about the number or the size of what was ordered. And then Beara -- and I say he's frustrated and pulling his hair out because then he just boldly says: "But I need 30 men, just like it was ordered." And then Krstic says: "Take from Nastic or Blagojevic." And you remember Nastic is the commander of the Milici Brigade; Blagojevic is the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Krstic says: "I can't pull anything out of here for you." This is day two of the attack on Zepa where Krstic had to send his best unit, Pandurevic, back to Zvornik, so Krstic isn't being really generous with his troops at this point for Beara and the murder operation. Then Beara responds: "But I don't have any here. I need them today and I'll give them back tonight, Krle." That's Krstic's nickname. These guys know each other. "You have to understand. I can't explain it to you like this. Krstic: "I'll disturb everything on his axis if I pull them out and a lot depends on him." So axis, if you know, axis of attack. Krstic is concerned about his attack on Zepa. And then Beara says openly: "I can't resolve anything without 15 to 30 men and Boban Indzic." Now, we've learned from Butler and other evidence in this case, Boban Indzic is an officer from Visegrad. And then Krstic says: "Ljubo, this is not protected." Clearly they both know this is an unprotected line and they're arrogant officers and they just can't help themselves. I don't know why they're doing it but they do. Beara says: "I know, I know." And then Krstic goes on, talks more about Nastic and Blagojevic. And then interestingly Beara says: "But I don't have any. If I did, I wouldn't still be asking for the third day." Now, I'm not great with arithmetic, but if he's asking for this on the 15th and it's the third day, the 13th would be the day that he originally asked for these troops and, of course, that's the day we know that thousands of Muslim prisoners are arriving and need to be dealt with. Then Krstic goes back to Blagojevic and his Red Berets and go to the MUP, the Ministry of Interior. Beara responds: "No, they won't do anything. I talked to them. There's no other solution but for 15 to 30 men." Now Beara is negotiating. He's gone from 60. Now he needs 15 to 30. And then he says: "The thing that was supposed to arrive on the 13th but didn't." Okay, boom, that confirms that's when he was asking, that's when he got the order, that's when they were supposed to arrive. And then Krstic: "Ljubo you have to understand me, you've done fucking all sorts to me." Something like that. And Beara: "I understand, but have you to understand me too. Had this been done, we wouldn't be arguing -- had this been done then, we wouldn't be arguing over it now. Beara can't argue with Krstic either. Krstic: "Fuck it, now I'll be the one to blame." They're both scared of Mladic that they're going to blame them for not taking part in the murder operation. Beara: "I don't know what to do. I mean it, Krle. There are still 3500 parcels that I have to distribute and I have no solution. "Fuck it, I'll see what I can do." After that, over 800 men were killed that afternoon at Kozluk by elements of the Rocevic Battalion. But then on 16th, over 1700 men were killed at Branjevo Farm by the 10th Sabotage Detachment and people from Bratunac. Now, lastly, so there's no concern that Furtula didn't carry out Mladic's orders, we'll see the last -- the last intercept, P1285. Importantly at 1919 hours. We don't know who these guys are, but you can see that someone is looking for a bus and to send the bus towards Visegrad, Podromanija, Rogatica, and further on. That is way down if you look at a map, well beyond down past these areas, a long distance from Bratunac. When he comes across a bus with a group of soldiers, those are the ones from Visegrad, Boban is their commander: "Say again? "Here they are again. "Boban Indzic, and then bring them to the command in Bratunac." Now, those guys, evening's coming, sitting by a broken bus in the afternoon, soldiers, just -- who knows where they went, but they didn't see Beara. Those compelling intercepts leave no doubt whatsoever, Mladic is issuing orders pursuant to the murder operation. Now, finally, I would like to conclude my remarks with some words to the women of Srebrenica and others that have suffered and continue to suffer from Mladic's crimes. But it is the Srebrenica and Zepa women where my team have for over 20 years spoken to you, listened to you, and learned from you, and we've been privileged to bring some of you here to The Hague to share with this Tribunal your experience, your pain, and your incredible courage, facing down the people that committed this genocide. We have also spoken to your precious few men and boys who survived the killing fields from Kravica to Branjevo. From all of you, we have learned so much. One thing we've learned about your husbands and your sons was their fear of not being able to say good-bye to you, and we know you felt and still feel that terrible pain. So I looked and looked for someone who may have been able to put something down on a scrap of paper or something for you; but, of course, they were never given a chance to even hold a pencil. I did find something though. I had to go to another place, another time, another terrible war, but I found a letter from a husband, a soldier, who was able to say good-bye to his wife, and I believe his words and feelings are those your husbands and sons and brothers would have sent to you had they had a chance. I'll read you parts of this letter that was written on the 14th of July, 1861. "My very dear Sarah, "The indications are very strong that we shall move in a few days, perhaps tomorrow. Lest I should not be able to write you again, I feel impelled to write lines that may fall under your eye when I shall be no more. ... "If it is necessary that I should fall on the battle-field, I am ready. I have no misgivings about, or lack of confidence in, the cause in which I am engaged, and my courage does not halt or falter. ... "But, my dear wife, when I know that with my own joys I lay down nearly all of yours and replace them in this life with cares and sorrows. As for our little boys, they will grow up as I have done, and never know a father's love and care. God's blessing upon them. "Sarah, my love for you is deathless, it seems to bind me to you with mighty cables that nothing but omnipotence could break. The memories of the blissful moments I have spent with you come creeping over me, and I feel most gratified to God and to you that I have enjoyed them so long. And hard it is for me to give them up and burn to ashes the hopes of future years, when God willing, we might still have lived and loved together and seen our sons grow up to honourable manhood around us... My dear Sarah, never forget how much I love you, and when my last breath escapes me on the battle-field, it will whisper your name. "Forgive my many faults, and the many pains I have caused you. How thoughtless and foolish I have oftentimes been. How gladly would I wash out with my tears every little spot upon your happiness and struggle with all the misfortunes of this world, to shield you and my children from harm. But I cannot. I must watch you from the spirit land and hover near you, while you buffet the storms with your precious little freight, and wait with sad patience till we meet to part no more. "But, oh, Sarah, if the dead can come back to this earth and flit unseen around those they loved, I shall always be near you; in the garish day and in the darkest night, amidst your happiest scenes and gloomiest hours - always, always; and if there be a soft breeze upon your cheek, it shall be my breath, or the cool air fans your throbbing temple, it shall be my spirit passing by. Sarah, do not mourn me dead; think I am gone and wait for me, for we shall meet again." Sullivan Ballou died one week later in a place called Bull Run. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No one can fathom the extent of the individual tragedies of the victims in this case. The children torn from mother's arms to be killed, the starving prisoners beaten to death over a period of days with rifle-butts, clubs, boots, the women and girls raped, sexually abused over and over, the daily terror of waiting for a bullet or a shell, those who survived physically intact but struggle with the memories of lost loves ones, lost homes, lost communities. The litany of tragedies goes on and on and on. No one can fathom the extent of the sufferings for which Ratko Mladic is responsible. So in the face of that, what does one say and what must one ignore to argue that Mladic should receive less than the most severe sentence? You say, as we see at paragraph 3394 of the Defence brief, that Mladic's sentence should be reduced because of his "benevolent treatment" of victims; for example, he "facilitated the achievement of an agreement on the demilitarization of the areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, thus reaffirming his will to establish peace and the applicability of the Geneva Conventions." And you ignore that this was forced on him, as he complained in P1793: "If the international community had not meddled, they," that is Muslims, "would have paid the price." And you ignore that he chafed under this restraint, as he told his companion on the tour of destroyed Muslim villages that we saw in the video on Monday morning, if the international forces, now the Dutch, "would not protect them, they," Muslims, "would have disappeared from this area long ago." And you ignore his relish at finally overcoming the restraint when he entered Srebrenica. "Now the time has come to take revenge on the Turks." Or you claim, Your Honours, that his sentence should be reduced because he purchased candy for children in Potocari. That's at paragraph 3397. And you ignore that this alleged purchase of candy was for the kids whose fathers, uncles and brothers he was about to murder. Or you assert that his sentence should be limited because of alleged SFRY sentencing practices, and you ignore that four of Mladic's subordinates - Popovic, Beara, Tolimir, Galic - received life sentences for executing his orders for only a fraction of the crimes for which he is responsible for; sentences that were affirmed on appeal. You try to paint Mladic as a man who "never intended to cause suffering" but instead "took concrete steps to avoid suffering where possible" and that the conduct of the accused has saved many lives and, therefore, a reduction of sentence is warranted. That's at paragraphs 3395 and 3398. And you ignore that this is not the first time that Mladic has tried to depict himself as a saver of lives. Recall P1147, that's a video, V000-9268, at 7:41 through 8:42, that's video footage from Zepa in 1995 of General Mladic ostentatiously boarding buses to advise the petrified occupants, in the process of being expelled, that "now I am giving you your life as a gift. I forgive you all and am giving you your life as a present." Ratko Mladic, the master of life and death, basking in self-praise and demanding gratitude from those whose lives he decided to spare. And now here in court, denying responsibility for those he did kill, blaming the subordinates who executed his orders and deservedly received the most severe sentence for doing so. Because the magnitude of these crimes admit of nothing more than the most severe penalty available under law, the only thing one can really argue in support of a sentence less than that most severe is that he didn't commit the crimes. And so that is what the Defence does in its sentencing submissions, arguing at paragraphs 3393 and 3401 that "... any crimes that may have been committed were the result of disobeying individuals acting outside of their duties." Or that General Mladic was a "professional with knowledge of the laws of war that he always sought to apply in the most ethical manner." But these crimes did occur. They happened to one person after another, one person at a time, one father, one wife, one grandmother, one tradesman, one student, one doctor. One after another after another after another. And at paragraph 1743 of our brief, you can find just the tiniest fraction, representative fraction, of illustrations reflecting both the vulnerability of these victims and the depths of the suffering they endured and continue to suffer. The time has come for General Mladic to be held accountable for those crimes against each of his victims and the communities he destroyed. It would be incompatible with Tribunal sentencing practice, an insult to the victims, living and dead, and an affront to justice to impose any sentence other than the most severe available under law: A life sentence. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. That concludes the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We'll in a second adjourn for the day. Is there any chance that a response to the latest sentencing-related motion of the Defence would be received before Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly before Friday. That has been our objective. We'll try to get it out today, and if not, first thing tomorrow morning, I would think that we can achieve that. Is that -- would that be sufficient time for the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think most important is that if we have received a response, we can consider it. And I have got no idea what the response will be, but it may have an impact on what the Defence wants to use in their final argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I say, if at all possible, we'll get it out, filed today and, if not, first thing tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Friday, the 9th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
